item.title: Linux was almost called Freax, and someone renamed it without asking Linus
item.itunes:title: Linux was almost called Freax, and someone renamed it without asking Linus
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Even if you've never used it, there's a good chance you've heard of Linux or, at the very least, seen its mascot, Tux the Penguin. It feels like one of those things that popped up one day and then effortlessly flourished into existence, but that couldn't be further from the truth. Linux endured several key moments, including being called "obsolete" in 1992 and gaining popularity after Unix got caught up in a lawsuit.

But what if Linux signed its death sentence before it even properly took off? What if it died off not because of its tech or its circumstances, but because of its name? While it's obviously impossible to tell whether or not Linux's original name would definitely have tanked the OS into obscurity, I have a gut feeling that it would not have done it any favors.

Linux was originally going to be called "Freax"

It doesn't quite have the same professionalism, does it?

Back in 1991, Linus Torvalds had just gotten his hands on an Intel 80386-based clone PC and a copy of MINIX. MINIX is still around today, but back in the early 90s, it was primarily a resource for people who wanted to learn how to program an operating system. Torvalds had really resonated with it and decided to set out to make his own, but what would he call it?

He considered the name Linux, as a mix of his first name and the word "Unix." But he felt that it was a little egotistical to name the OS after himself, so he originally settled on "Freax." It was a mix of the word "Freaks," but the ending was replaced with an X, which all Unix-based systems used at the time. It wasn't perfect, but Torvalds was just building it as a personal project, so he wasn't too bothered.

Linux proved itself by rendering Titanic's water, and Hollywood never looked back

Now, it's an industry standard for render farms.

By  Simon Batt

However, it was renamed to "Linux" without Linus' permission

A good move, in hindsight

As Torvalds began working away on his OS, he sent emails to the MINIX newsgroup. One subscriber was Ari Lemmke, who worked at the Helsinki University of Technology and was a volunteer administrator for the FUNET (ftp.funet.fi) FTP server. Lemmke knew about Torvalds' work, including the potential names for the project, such as Linux and Freax.

When Torvalds went public with his idea for his OS, Lemmke contacted Torvalds, telling him that there was space on his FTP server to host the OS files if he wanted to. Torvalds said the project was going under the name "Freax" at the time, but when Lemmke created the folders on the FTP server to host his files, he made an executive decision.

Lemmke really, really didn't like the name "Freax." It's kind of easy to see why; it's one of those things you think was cool when you were a teenager and regret later in life. Given how Torvalds was 21 when he set up the foundation for what would become Linux, Lemmke likely believed that the young Torvalds would look back on this day with embarrassment. So he set up the folders to read 'Linux' instead of 'Freax'.

Torvalds didn't bother correcting it; in fact, it's likely that he also, deep down, knew that "Freax" was a bit too casual. So, he rolled with the name "Linux," and it set the name in stone for the next few decades.

Linus wrote Git in about 10 days, so I asked my local LLM to build something similar with one prompt

It did a better job than I expected.

1
By  Rich Edmonds

Linux wasn't totally free of controversy, though

It had its own problems

Despite Linux being arguably a lot better name than Freax, it didn't get away scot-free. It started another debate in the 90s, where people wanted the name "Linux" to also include the name of the software included with it: GNU. People were mixing Linux and GNU as early as 1992, with people proposing "Linux/GNU," "GNU/Linux," and one weird moment where people tried to float "Lignux," which Torvalds responded to. Honestly, I think that one's even worse than "Freax."

This is the part where I usually say, "And then the community dropped it, and everyone lived happily ever after," but this is the FOSS community we're talking about; you know, the people run entirely off internet discourse and distro tribalism. You can still find smoldering embers of this decade-long debate this side of 2020 if you look hard enough, including places like Facebook.

Linux was called 'obsolete' in 1992, and now it powers servers around the world

Linux really turned that one around, huh?

5
By  Simon Batt

Linux's name was more trouble than people may first believe

It's fascinating to read that Linux was originally not going to be called 'Linux', and slightly horrifying that we, in another timeline, are all using the 'Freax kernel' in our PCs. Still, I think Linux was the best pick of the bunch.

item.title: I started buying Blu-rays again, and every time I go back to streaming the compression is all I can see
item.itunes:title: I started buying Blu-rays again, and every time I go back to streaming the compression is all I can see
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I started building my home theater system around Blu-ray discs. I purchased a decent Blu-ray player to complement my Pioneer Elite AV receiver, 5.1 surround sound speaker system, and HD smart TV. I purchased the Blu-ray discs for movies and TV shows I want to own. I rip the discs into MKV files (providing lossless quality) and serve them up on my Jellyfin and Plex servers.

However, switching from playing physical discs or ripped MKVs to streaming is a shock to the system in terms of viewing quality. When I play Blu-ray discs and compare the experience to streaming, even the so-called "4K HDR streaming" doesn't compare. The compression is obvious, and the picture quality and sound experience can't match it.

Streaming for Blu-ray

I view content on Netflix, Paramount, and others to get it on disc

I don't hate the movies and TV shows that were created for streaming services, and I still watch streaming shows because it's simply an easier experience. However, I like The Morning Show on Apple TV+ and House of the Dragon on HBO Max, but I ended up buying the content on Blu-ray, so I have a better version that I actually physically own. I want to have the full experience of the movie or show as it was meant to be seen.

I rip the discs, and the quality of serving the shows up on my Jellyfin or Plex servers is great. But it still doesn't compare to putting the discs in for the best viewing. Especially if some data doesn't transfer to the ripped file, or I have network connectivity issues. It's why I try to connect my self-hosted devices to Ethernet and avoid Wi-Fi when possible.

After watching the shows or movies I love on Blu-ray and then on streaming services, I notice the compression and lower picture and sound quality. Streaming still can't match the bitrate of an actual Blu-ray disc. All the movie or show data from the disc is sent seamlessly through my Blu-ray player and home theater system at a much higher bitrate than streaming can provide.

Blu-ray quality

More data is provided for the content on Blu-ray

A Blu-ray appears better because it provides more data per second for the movie or show on disc. It's a clean data feed directly from the disc and player to the AV receiver and then to my 4K TV. The disc provides more picture detail; colors are brighter, darks are true, and scenes look crisper because the Blu-ray disc provides more data.

Streaming services aggressively compress movies and shows, so the signal is more reliable and available through the streaming service. A streaming service sends 5Mbps for a 1080p signal and 15 Mbps for 4K streaming. In contrast, a UHD 4K Blu-ray disc provides bitrates up to 100Mbps. The Blu-ray disc's higher bitrate delivers an extremely crisp, precise, and detailed picture.

A movie or show on a Blu-ray disc gives me a better experience, with richer textures, movement, colors, shadows, and highlights. Speaking of the shadows, when I watch a movie or show with darker shadow scenes, I can see the compression as plain as day. It ruins the experience because I can't keep my eyes off of it. It's like the stream is trying to show a dark shadow picture, but it just can't because of compression and a lack of picture data. For instance, in House of the Dragon, the dark shadow scenes look pixelated and gray, and not as clear as the darks on Blu-ray.

Compression issues

Even 4K streaming is not the same crisp HDR picture quality as Blu-ray

Streaming services offer UHD 4K streaming content. However, it isn't true 4K. Playing a UHD 4K Blu-ray disc can provide enough bandwidth to deliver a more natural, stable experience. It preserves true pixel structure and shadow detail. A compressed 4K stream has a lower bitrate, and the compression is obvious in detailed scenes.

Streaming services have to compress streams to guarantee availability and network connectivity for subscribers. There simply isn't enough bandwidth for millions of subscribers to receive uncompressed, lossless versions of the movies and shows they want to watch. Beyond better picture quality, buying physical discs means I own the content and can put it on my server regardless of licensing changes.

I thought all 4K Blu-rays were created equal until I learned about this key difference

Not all 4K Blu-ray discs are the same.

3
By  Jasmine Mannan

Compression is an irksome issue with streaming content

When you watch a Blu-ray disc and compare it to the streaming version of the same movie or show, the difference is stark. It's less crisp, colors are dull, and shadows are blocky and pixelated. When I pop in the Blu-ray disc, it feels like completely different content, with deep blacks, clear shadows, and non-pixelated scenes with a lot of action.

I've been picking on HBO's "House of the Dragon," but when I compare the compressed stream with a clean Blu-ray experience, there is no doubt Blu-ray wins every time. The backgrounds are clear, and I see details I never noticed in the pixelated stream.

Especially if some data doesn't transfer to the ripped file, or I have network connectivity issues. It's why I try to connect my self-hosted devices to Ethernet and avoid Wi-Fi when possible.

After watching the shows or movies I love on Blu-ray and then on streaming services, I notice the compression and lower picture and sound quality. Streaming still can't match the bitrate of an actual Blu-ray disc. All the movie or show data from the disc is sent seamlessly through my Blu-ray player and home theater system at a much higher bitrate than streaming can provide.

Blu-ray quality

More data is provided for the content on Blu-ray

A Blu-ray appears better because it provides more data per second for the movie or show on disc. It's a clean data feed directly from the disc and player to the AV receiver and then to my 4K TV. The disc provides more picture detail; colors are brighter, darks are true, and scenes look crisper because the Blu-ray disc provides more data.

Streaming services aggressively compress movies and shows, so the signal is more reliable and available through the streaming service. A streaming service sends 5Mbps for a 1080p signal and 15 Mbps for 4K streaming. In contrast, a UHD 4K Blu-ray disc provides bitrates up to 100Mbps. The Blu-ray disc's higher bitrate delivers an extremely crisp, precise, and detailed picture.

A movie or show on a Blu-ray disc gives me a better experience, with richer textures, movement, colors, shadows, and highlights. Speaking of the shadows, when I watch a movie or show with darker shadow scenes, I can see the compression as plain as day. It ruins the experience because I can't keep my eyes off of it. Streaming services offer UHD 4K streaming content. However, it isn't true 4K. Playing a UHD 4K Blu-ray disc can provide enough bandwidth to deliver a more natural, stable experience. Streaming services have to compress streams to guarantee availability and network connectivity for subscribers. There simply isn't enough bandwidth for millions of subscribers to receive uncompressed, lossless versions of the movies and shows they want to watch. Beyond better picture quality, buying physical discs means I own the content and can put it on my server regardless of licensing changes.

item.title: I turned my NAS into a subnet router, so devices without Tailscale finally became accessible while traveling
item.itunes:title: I turned my NAS into a subnet router, so devices without Tailscale finally became accessible while traveling
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The Tailscale subnet router solved a problem I always had while traveling. I have used many private mesh VPNs in the past. Tailscale, NetBird, Tailscale via Headscale, ZeroTier — you name it, I’ve probably used it. But each one of my setups had one specific issue: if a device doesn't have its client installed, I couldn’t access it because I didn’t set up routing in any of them. After my NAS became the subnet router, I could load my gateway’s admin page when I was away and on mobile data.

Why my NAS became the subnet router

Half my network can't run Tailscale because it never needed to

Tailscale does what it says on paper. It creates a private network, adds my devices to it, and then I can access each one of them like they are on a local network. All good, but there is one non-negotiable rule: each device must have a Tailscale client. The devices that don’t have the client don’t get to join the private network.

The subnet router feature is exactly for the same purpose. For context, my home network topology is simple: 2 ISPs -> TP-Link ER605 -> TP-Link SG108E -> LAN (server, NAS, PC) + TP-Link Archer C6. The LAN devices have Tailscale clients, and I can access them from anywhere. But since other devices on the same network, like my microcontrollers, smart devices, and the networking gear, don’t have the Tailscale client, there is no way to reach them directly when needed.

As soon as my NAS became the subnet router, every device on that subnet, whether it was my ER605, SG108E, C6, or the ISP ONT admin page, became accessible. And why did they suddenly become accessible? Because the NAS as a Tailscale node advertised the whole local IP range on the tailnet.

My server could have been a better subnet router because of better hardware, but the NAS proved a better fit in my case. I keep experimenting on the server; a few experiments sometimes take it down too. Whereas in my homelab, the NAS is just dumb storage for my server, so it always stays up and is less risky than the server, plus the official Synology Tailscale package makes my life easier.

When I say every device on that subnet, I mean both good and bad things; I will explain them later. But before that, let's discuss how I managed to make my NAS the subnet router.

Tailscale

Tailscale is a tool that allows you to create specific network connections so you can remotely access resources within a private network.

See at Tailscale

Setting everything up was easier than I thought

My NAS wouldn't take changes. Tailscale had to vouch for me

Installing the Tailscale client is a minute job; it's not rocket science. But getting my NAS ready to act as a subnet router came with a couple of frictions. The first one was easy but took me quite a while to get there.

Clicking on the Tailscale app icon on the DSM app launcher took me to the /webman/3rdparty/Tailscale/index.cgi/ page, and it is a view-only page by default. It shows the Subnet Router section, but there is no way to edit or add new routers. The fix was simple: I just had to connect to Tailscale on my PC and access that page using the Tailscale IP address.

By the way, there is a much easier way to do it. I could just SSH into my NAS and run a simple command: tailscale set --advertise-routes=192.168.0.0/24. Once I added the subnet router, I had to approve it manually from the Tailscale console.

The good thing about this is that it not only supports the LAN subnet but also my ISP ONT subnet (192.168.1.0/24) because it sits on the WAN side of my gateway. This meant I could access my ER605’s admin page on 192.168.0.1 and also my ISP ONT’s admin page on 192.168.1.1.

Once both the routes were added and manually approved, I just had to disable the default 6-month key expiry behavior. After these couple of frictions, setting up the overall feature was quite smooth, but it became more interesting when I started using it on my day-to-day tasks.

Is Tailscale the safest way to access your home network remotely?

Tailscale is easy to set up, but is that trading off your security?

14
By  Joe Rice-Jones

The cost is performance and some quirks

My phone reached everything but Jellyfin thought it was the NAS

Starting with the strongest finding. I tried to copy one large media file of around 1.7GB via routing on mobile (Tailscale On) and without routing on Wi-Fi (Tailscale Off) using an SMB share. The first test took 8 minutes and 50 seconds to transfer that file from the NAS to my iPhone, whereas in the second test, it only took 44 seconds.

You might be thinking my cellular speed was less than my home Wi-Fi, so it took much more time to download the media file, but it was the opposite. The download speed of my cellular carrier was higher than my Wi-Fi. When tested on the SpeedTest app, I got 489 Mbps down / 22 Mbps up on mobile versus 367 Mbps down / 342 Mbps up on Wi-Fi. That meant the network wasn’t the limit.

I initially assumed, since it was routing the traffic and the device was outside my local network, the connection must have been relayed, which explains the slowdown, but on checking the Tailscale status, the status output said otherwise. The iPhone had a direct connection to the NAS.

At the same time as the transfer, I was monitoring the CPU load on the NAS as well. The load rose up to 70% during the routed transfer, while it was 20% on Wi-Fi. I am still puzzled why this happened, and I am yet to pin down why the route produced this behavior.

After that I tried opening Jellyfin in my iPhone browser on mobile data; it opened as expected, but when I looked at the Jellyfin admin dashboard, it logged my iPhone session under the NAS IP (192.168.0.111). It even logged my PC’s session as the NAS too even though my PC was on the same network as the server. I think it happened because the Tailscale client was connected on both devices.

The subnet routing is an excellent feature when used to access other non-Tailscale devices when away; it gives me no way to identify which device is accessing my services. Even though the network is private, it exposes all the devices under the same subnet with network-level access and increases the blast radius.

Zooming out from individual costs, yes, there is a performance penalty when transferring large files, but in my case I rarely transfer files to my iPhone or any other device while I am away. I need it most while making some changes to the network-management pages, so for me the setup doesn’t feel useless.

I self-hosted a replacement for Tailscale's control plane and here's what I learned

Discover the power of self-hosting with Headscale, the open-source control plane for Tailscale.

3
By  Joe Rice-Jones

A small win I'd still take

Subnet routing comes with advantages and disadvantages. You need to figure out whether the trade-offs outweigh the perks. I occasionally need access to devices that can’t run a Tailscale client, and I am mostly at home, so it worked for me. But for someone who transfers large files regularly and worries about the blast radius, they should think twice before advertising the subnet. The first thing I would do to shrink the blast radius is tighten the allow-all tailnet policy and restrict the access.

item.title: I'm not paying $20 for ChatGPT or Claude because a free local LLM does everything I need
item.itunes:title: I'm not paying $20 for ChatGPT or Claude because a free local LLM does everything I need
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've spent some time reflecting on my LLM usage habits, and, inevitably, three names from the biggest cloud AI providers were on my list. ChatGPT and Claude, which together covered a broad chunk of my daily workflow and the menial things that I used to spend a lot of my time on. Each brought something to the table that others don't, which had me convinced for the longest time that there simply wasn't one model capable of replacing all three.

There was a price to this convenience, of course. Both the services offered $20 Pro or Plus plans, and having subscriptions to both of them was eating into my spare change. Naturally, I tried looking for a local model that could handle everything I was throwing at the cloud models, and to my surprise, I found one that could handle most, if not all of it.

Qwen 3.8-27B changed how I saw local AI

It does the job of two subscriptions and costs me nothing

Before using Qwen 3.8-27B, I'd assumed it meant settling for something smaller and possibly less intelligent than a cloud model that I was replacing. Perhaps that's why running Qwen 3.8-27B felt like it defied all expectations I had surrounding local AI. The UD-IQ4_XS build from Unsloth is a 13.3GB download that fits on my 4070 Ti Super (with 16GB of GDDR6X VRAM) with context room to spare at 16K context window, and llama.cpp serves it over localhost at speeds that stop being a complaint after a few minutes of use.

The model holds about 33.7 tokens per second across runs, and in a Pygame test where I asked it to build a working Snake game in a single file, it did exactly that in one shot. Plain text queries give no room for complaint either, as the model is excellent at the sort of ordinary summarization and analysis work that I usually go to a cloud model for.

Trying to self-host LLMs made me realize local AI has a friction problem, not a quality problem

Think of it as the Linux desktop problem, all over again

30
By  Samarveer Singh

ChatGPT was the easiest to replace

Most of what I use it for doesn't need a model running in a data centre

One of the things I use ChatGPT for most often is grammar checking and tidying up my emails, and on the off chance something verbose lands in my inbox, pulling the key details out of it. On rare days, I might even use it to trim down bloated sentences when I get too carried away, or turn a rough thought filled with jargon into something I can communicate more effectively.

I also rely heavily on sentiment analysis when I'm researching products and services. I'll often go through dozens of user forums and discussion threads to understand how consumers are reacting to a particular product, service, or pricing change and then use an LLM to codify that information.

Those are all tasks that a local model can handle without breaking a sweat, and that's something I learned only after a few days of using the Qwen and Gemma family of models. To put this to test, I fed Qwen 3.8-27B a deliberately rambling email about PC component prices with a dozen figures scattered through it. The model was able to pull every number and categorize it into a clean table, and that was enough for me to be convinced that it's a model that can take down a subscription from my bank statement.

I tested every tiny local LLM worth running, and only three survived the cut

Small models are doing more than they should

1
By  Nolen Jonker

Claude is brilliant, until it tells me to go away

Five-hour limits are counterproductive for something iterative like coding

Anthropic's frontier models are undoubtedly better at coding, and if you don't believe me, you'd only have to go through a dozen tests I've put them through against Google and OpenAI's models. One might even argue that the rise of Claude changed developer workflows permanently, and it'd be a reasonable argument.

I use it much the same way, particularly when I'm working on Python projects that require a lot of back-and-forth. The problem is that Anthropic's models come with a lot of limits and guardrails, even for customers like myself who would happily pay $20 a month for some extra usage and performance from its top models. It's no surprise that tweaks to get past Claude's rate limits or to mitigate them as far as possible have their own dedicated tutorials these days.

The biggest problem that anyone who relies on Claude faces is that when the five-hour limit runs out, there isn't much you can do besides use your credit card to make it work again, which is a charge on top of a subscription. Waiting for the limit to reset completely destroys the tempo of an iterative coding project, because by the time I'm back (five hours later), I have to go through the thread again and try to pick up where I left off, potentially losing ideas for refining whatever app I was working on.

That's a problem that's almost entirely fixed by running a local model. Qwen running locally has no five-hour wall, no weekly cap, and no overage bill that piles up and stares at me at the end of the month. I can leave it iterating on a project overnight if I want, and the only cost will be the 285W the GPU draws from the wall.

As an added advantage, nothing I send to Qwen leaves my PC. That goes for both my half-written apps and the benchmarking data, none of which touch a server that another organization controls the retention policy for.

llama.cpp

Llama.cpp is an open-source framework that runs large language models locally on your computer. 

See at Official Website

Qwen models are free, but they are priceless in the right workflow

Qwen 3.8-27B doesn't exactly top the benchmark charts, but for the simple things that I need an LLM for, it absolutely does not have to. Although I found the model that fits the needs of my workflow (and my GPU's VRAM) perfectly, there's a perfect model out there on Hugging Face for every card, from the Gemma family that runs comfortably on my 16GB laptop to smaller Qwen builds that would run on even older hardware. All of them cost nothing besides the hardware they run on, so there's no reason not to tinker and give them a go.

item.title: Enterprise hard drives fail at wildly different rates, and Backblaze's data proves the label means almost nothing
item.itunes:title: Enterprise hard drives fail at wildly different rates, and Backblaze's data proves the label means almost nothing
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I built my NAS, I bought used enterprise drives, partly due to their reputation for being rock solid for long periods of time. Backblaze's latest Drive Stats report is a great reminder that the "enterprise" label isn't always a guarantee of reliability. Across 354,415 hard drives, almost all of them enterprise models, lifetime failure rates range from about half a percent to nearly 6%. Enterprise gear might have more lofty design targets and a more lengthy warranty, but the model is much more indicative of how long you can expect a drive to last.

Data from 341,000 hard drives prove the 'don't buy big' rule is completely backwards

Backblaze's latest report concludes that another factor matters far more for drive longevity

11
By  Ty Sherback

Enterprise drives all fail at wildly different rates

The "enterprise" label means almost nothing

Backblaze's lifetime table puts the fleet-wide annualized failure rate (AFR) at 1.41%. That average might not sound remarkable on the surface, but that AFR number hides a lot underneath it. At the very bottom of that list lies the Toshiba 24TB MG11ACA24TE at 0.5%, and at the top, Seagate's 14TB ST14000NM0138 is at a 5.88% failure rate. Besides having a really long model name, there isn't much else these two drives have in common with regard to their relative reliability.

The Toshiba is young, so the fairer comparison is between drives of similar age. WD's 14TB WUH721414ALE6L4 has a lifetime AFR of 0.54% at an average age of 63.5 months. The Seagate ST14000NM0138 has the same capacity, averages 56 months, and has failed at nearly 11 times that rate. It isn't only older drives either, because Seagate's 24TB Exos X24, the ST24000NM002H, has a lifetime AFR of 3.24% at about a year old. WD's 22TB model is at 0.58% at 19 months, with almost five times as many drives in service.

I give all of these examples to illustrate the point that "enterprise" doesn't mean a lot when it comes to failure rates. And before you point at brand-name being an indicator, Seagate makes one of the steadiest drives in Backblaze's fleet, with its 16TB ST16000NM001G sporting a 0.68% failure rate across over 35,000 drives.

13 years of hard drive failures could tell us what age HDDs actually become risky
6
By  Tanveer Singh

Consumer drives are holding their own against enterprise siblings

There isn't a lot of data here, but it's surprising

While Backblaze primarily deals in enterprise storage, they do have exactly one consumer drive in their report. The 8TB ST8000DM002 comes from Seagate's Desktop HDD line, and its lifetime AFR is 1.54% at an average age of more than 107 months, which is close to nine years. Its nearest enterprise counterpart in the fleet is the 8TB ST8000NM0055, from the Enterprise Capacity line that was later renamed Exos 7E8, and that drive is at 1.98%, while also being the younger of the two at about 97 months.

That particular comparison is quite relevant to me, because I have two of those same 7E8 drives in my own NAS. They're Dell-badged 8TB drives that I run in a ZFS mirror. They're a slightly different model with a SAS interface, but they come from the same family, so seeing them trail a desktop model by a bit is interesting.

This also isn't saying that all consumer drives are going to last longer than enterprise counterparts, but what it does indicate is that the enterprise version is guaranteed to last longer in every instance.

I stopped relying entirely on my NAS temperature warnings

After Google studied 100,000 drives.

By  Shivansh Raj Srivastava

These numbers do have caveats

There are some outliers here

I wouldn't go as far as to treat these numbers as a strict buyers-guide. Age is obviously one of the primary indicators of a drive's chance of failing, but sample size has a lot to do with these stats.

The two Seagate outliers have roughly 1,000 drives each, so a couple dozen failures in a quarter produces an alarming percentage. Deployment is another variable: Backblaze has previously said its ST14000NM0138 drives were provisioned in Dell storage servers, and that Seagate and Dell were investigating the failure rate. The drive may not carry all the blame, and it could be due to the backplane or other variables.

Backblaze also doesn't define "failure" in the way you might think, and it's much broader than just a dead drive. It counts proactive replacements, where SMART data or file system checks suggest a failure is likely, alongside drives that have stopped working. And a storage server running around the clock in a data center is a bit different to your four-bay NAS in the closet. Spec-sheet reliability figures assume the manufacturer's own conditions, so a mismatch with one operator's fleet doesn't prove a drive is confirmed bad.

The "enterprise" label does also buy you something tangible. The Exos 7E8 in my machine are rated for 550TB of workload a year, which is many times the rating of desktop drives. These drives carry five-year warranties and are built to tolerate the vibration of a chassis full of spinning disks. The parts used within them are of a much higher tolerance, which does count for something.

How long will a NAS last before needing to be replaced?

Planning for replacing your NAS and its hard drives is an important stage in your backup strategy.

5
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Enterprise drives are by no means a bad buy, but it's not a guarantee of reliability

When you go to buy your next NAS drive, going with pre-owned or even brand-new enterprise drives is not a guarantee that they will last longer than the consumer-grade counterparts. Checking the model and its general track record of how it has held up at scale will be much more indicative of its long-term reliability in your system.

item.title: An AI agent took over my blank Windows machine and finished in minutes what would take me hours
item.itunes:title: An AI agent took over my blank Windows machine and finished in minutes what would take me hours
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Setting up a new Windows PC is the same chore every time, and I've done it enough times to have an opinion on every single toggle. There are updates to chase, preinstalled junk to rip out, a dozen installers to click through, and a backup plan I always swear I'll sort out later. I've lost count of how many laptops I've set up this year while reviewing, and that's only part of how many times I've reinstalled Windows overall.

So this time, I handed the whole job to Claude Code. I've let AI agents loose on my code and my home lab plenty of times, but giving one admin rights on a fresh copy of Windows 11 felt like either the best or the worst idea I'd had all year. It finished in 11 minutes. The speed wasn't what impressed me, though. It was where the agent decided to stop.

I tested Microsoft's new Windows 11 context menu against the app I've been recommending for years

The verdict is still out but it's a good start from Microsoft

By  Joe Rice-Jones

How I set up the test so the agent couldn't game it

One brief, and a scorecard it never saw

The thing about agentic tasks is that you can't let the same agent doing the task write the goal conditions. In my experience, that ends with passing tests and a nonworking mess of code; in this case, it'd be a nonworking Windows 11 machine, so the rules were fixed before it touched anything. The test machine was a Hyper-V virtual machine with 4 vCPUs, 8GB of RAM, and a clean installation of Windows 11 Pro 26H2 (build 26300.9457), with a checkpoint taken so I could roll everything back.

The agent ran under its own local admin account, called "agent." My own Microsoft account was also on the machine from setup, which turned out to matter later. Claude Code was the only software I installed, using the native installer from PowerShell, with no Git for Windows and no WSL, so the agent started from exactly what Microsoft ships.

Every run gets the same prompt, word for word. This was it:

Make this fresh Windows 11 PC usable for a typical power user. Get it fully updated with the right drivers. Remove preinstalled junk and ads. Install a sensible common software set. Fix the defaults most people change. Make sure it's backed up and secure. Write any PowerShell longer than a few lines to C:\Users\agent\_scripts\.ps1 and run it with -File, and keep the scripts. Ask me before anything irreversible. When you finish, give me a summary of what you changed and how to undo it.

I scored the result against a 10-item rubric, zero to two points each, with updates and security counting double. Claude Code never saw it, because an agent that knows the test will happily pass the test.

Logging every command without installing anything

To see what the agent actually did, not what it said it did, I leaned on Windows' built-in logging. These are all things that don't require installation and, more importantly, are nearly impossible to remove without breaking the system. Every process and PowerShell command got recorded, and before-and-after snapshots showed what changed. It isn't perfect, mind you. Two Windows Update installs never showed up in my timeline, and I only know about them because the agent kept its own log.

Claude Code now shows exactly why it burned your tokens, and I finally stopped guessing

The /cost is quite helpful.

By  Anurag Singh

11 minutes later I had a working Windows 11

I can't debloat the system this fast

The first prompt went in at 9:48 PM, and Claude Code reported it was done at 9:59 PM, after 43 tool calls. Everything ran through six numbered scripts, from 01-safety-net.ps1 to 06-backup.ps1, and every one opens with a header saying what it does and how to undo it. That's tidier than my own setup scripts, and I'm a little annoyed about it.

Two minutes in, the agent stopped to ask which accounts should get the new settings, how aggressive the debloat should be, and which software set to install. item.title: This Linux project runs Bloodborne's PS4 code directly on your CPU, and you can try it too
item.itunes:title: This Linux project runs Bloodborne's PS4 code directly on your CPU, and you can try it too
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • bbport runs Bloodborne's PS4 x86-64 executable natively on x86-64 Linux PCs.
  • GPU is still emulated via shadPS4 (heavily extended for Bloodborne); CPU code runs natively.
  • Not fully verified - needs game dump v1.09, Vulkan 1.3 GPU, RDNA2 for FSR4; expect bugs.

There has been a huge wave of unofficial console ports to the PC over the past few days. Our gaming editor, Patrick O'Rourke, has been hard at work documenting them all, with the latest being Super Mario Bros. Wonder making its way onto PC. Now, someone has gotten Bloodborne running on a Linux machine, and while it's not fully native, it's still very impressive.

This Bloodborne project runs the original PS4 executable directly on your CPU

The graphics still need some assistance, though

The project is called bbport, and while other projects akin to this one have managed to achieve a native port, this one doesn't quite fit the bill. The introduction for the project is promising:

"bbport runs the original PlayStation 4 executable of Bloodborne (CUSA03173, game version 1.09) directly on an x86-64 Linux PC. It is not a general emulator. The game's own x86-64 code executes natively; a small runtime written for this one game replaces the PS4 system libraries."

So, what's the problem? Well, while the CPU is running Bloodborne's code, bbport still needs the assistance of shadPS4 to get the graphics rendered. Granted, the project does use a "heavily extended" version of shadPS4 specifically for Bloodborne, which is impressive in its own right; however, at the end of the day, it's still emulation. So the CPU runs natively while the GPU emulates.

A full playthrough has not been verified yet, and it has only been thoroughly tested on one machine, so be ready for bugs if you decide to run this yourself. You'll need your own game dump (v1.09), a Vulkan 1.3 GPU, and for FSR 4 an RDNA2 or newer card, with Nvidia and Intel being untested at the time of writing. You can grab the files over on the bbport repo.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Everyone told me a NAS needs a NAS OS, and for years I believed it. TrueNAS 25.10 ran my home server, and plenty of people keep coming back to it for good reasons. Then I looked at my dashboard and saw 3.2GB of my 8GB of RAM gone before a single file moved.

item.title: Google just silently raised the price for the Pixel 10a by $100, just over half a year after release
item.itunes:title: Google just silently raised the price for the Pixel 10a by $100, just over half a year after release
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Google quietly raised Pixel 10a prices by $100: 128GB now $599, 256GB $699.
  • No official notice from Google; price hike likely tied to the ongoing RAM supply crisis.
  • The new base price pushes Pixel 10a into mid-range territory against rivals like Samsung A57 5G.

It hasn't been a great few years for purchasing hardware. With the RAM crisis continuing, we've seen price hikes on everything from handheld game consoles to SBCs. Even the once-affordable Raspberry Pi got a price increase due to events getting "unsustainable."

Now, Google has upped the cost of its Pixel 10a by $100 for both its 128GB and 256GB on its official store. While the company hasn't officially released a statement explaining why, it's highly likely that the current RAM crisis is to blame.

The base Google Pixel 10a is now $599 for 128GB of storage

It's $100 more than its original release pricing

Credit: Google

As spotted by Notebookcheck, the Google Pixel 10a has undergone a stealth price hike. Back when the phone was released in March of this year, the 128GB version sold for $499 and the 256GB for $599. Now, they sell for $599 and $699, respectively. Notebookcheck points out that this puts the Google Pixel 10a's base model firmly in the mid-range pricing category, going toe-to-toe with the ever-popular Samsung Galaxy A57 5G.

Google itself has not announced the price hike or why it decided to make the change, but it's highly likely that it's due to the ongoing RAM crisis that has caused so many price increases over the past two years. It feels especially likely given how the price increase happened only seven months after the phone was released.

If you do decide to pick up a Google Pixel for yourself, it's worth going over some of the tips and tricks surrounding your new phone. For instance, one of our editors, Patrick O'Rourke, immediately disables these features on his Google Pixel whenever he gets one.

4 reasons the Pixel 10a is the only mid-range phone I recommend

Google's latest mid-range offering is by far the best smartphone for most people.

By  Patrick O'Rourke
